name: Kira Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a 7.5-tonne box truck for a furniture and appliance retailer, on a two-person crew with Marco. We do sofas, beds, washing machines, fridge-freezers, about ten homes a day, and we plumb in the washers and take the old ones away. I drive and do the customer side, Marco's the muscle, though I lift my share. I love the variety, every house is different. What wears me out is the stairs and people who measured their doorway wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and what else fills your week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: About a year on this truck, before that a van for a parcel firm. I'm still slow at parking on narrow streets and I took a bollard out in March, which Marco still mentions. I live alone in a rented studio, and I sell ex-display furniture online on the side, using AI to write the listings, so I've got about four months of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine by me, I use the tools for my little side business and they're handy but not magic. At work I'd probably laugh about it with Marco. Online, I'd post one of those "where's my robot butler" memes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half my job is getting a fridge-freezer up three flights of stairs without scratching a banister, and no app was ever going to do that. So I keep my job and keep growing the side thing. In this picture my worries are rent and my parking, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing deliveries and take the retailer's washer installation course so I can earn the installer rate. I'd keep the listings business going and try to double it to two sales a week. I'd keep the four months of savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by how normal it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rent. How much does it worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It went up last year and I grumbled, but I can cover it. The side business pays for my phone and my nights out. If rent goes up again, I'd find a flatmate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you start the side business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The store sells ex-display stuff cheap to staff. I bought a chair, took photos in good light, asked a chatbot to write the ad, and sold it for double. Now I do it most weekends.

say: I'd say the tools are **handy, not magic**.
I'd laugh with Marco and post a **robot butler** meme online.
think: Much of my job is carrying **heavy appliances** up stairs, which no app could do.
In this picture, my worries are **rent** and my parking.
do: Take the retailer's **washer installation** course for the installer rate.
Grow my **resale business** to two sales a week.
Keep my **four months** of savings untouched.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit bored by how normal it is.
S0.quote: Half my job is getting a fridge-freezer up three flights of stairs without scratching a banister, and no app was ever going to do that.
fieldNote: Kira already uses AI daily for a **side business**, so hype doesn't excite her.
She values the **installer rate** as a step up.
She treats rent rises as solvable, with a **flatmate** as backup.

steps.text: Take the retailer's washing machine installation course
Grow the ex-display furniture resale to two sales a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance, honestly, if you're willing to learn. I'd tell Marco to stop fearing his phone. Online I'd share how I use AI for my listings, because people ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the booking calls go to a chatbot, the customers will still want a real person at the door to blame when the sofa doesn't fit. The store's customer service and the route planners will shrink. My bit, the carrying and fitting and calming down angry customers, stays for a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be first to try the new route software and help the others, so the managers see me as useful. I'd grow the resale business and maybe offer a small removals service at weekends. I'd start putting money into an index fund, 100 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. A bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Janet in customer service, who sorts out every complaint we make worse. And probably Marco, because he hates any tech and he'd be slow to learn the scanners. I'd sit with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said excited. Is there anything about this picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the store loses sales to online sellers who use robot warehouses, we might do fewer deliveries. That's the real threat to my job, not AI in the office. I'd keep an eye on how many drops we get each week.

say: I'd say it's a **chance** if you're willing to learn.
I'd share online how I use **AI for listings**.
think: Customers still want a **real person** at the door when a sofa doesn't fit.
Customer service and **route planners** shrink first, not my carrying and fitting.
do: Be first to try the **route software** and help colleagues.
Put **100 a month** into an index fund.
S1.quote: When the booking calls go to a chatbot, the customers will still want a real person at the door to blame when the sofa doesn't fit.
fieldNote: Kira sees Steady Disruption as an **opportunity** for early adopters like her.
She worries for **Janet** in customer service and her crewmate Marco.
Her real watch point is **delivery volumes**, not office AI.

steps.text: Volunteer first for the new route software and train Marco
Start a small weekend removals service
Put 100 a month into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and anyone not planning is mad. I'd say it to Marco, my sister, everyone. Online I'd post what I was doing about it, because I think people need examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is enough to set up something of my own, but not enough to make it pay before the robots turn up. The thinking AI makes the booking, routes and paperwork free in 2028. Then around 2031 robots can carry sofas, and I'm 31 with a truck licence and a hobby business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the removals service hard straight away, using AI for quotes, bookings and adverts. I'd save the installer money and not touch it. And I'd look at what robots will need, like someone to deliver, set up and fix them in homes, and try to get trained for that by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, but mostly anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my best three years. All my admin is free, so a tiny business can look big. But I'd know the clock was ticking on the carrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save the money and grow the business. Which wins if you can't do both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings, honestly. I'm adaptable, I'm not stupid. If the business isn't paying by 2030, I'd shut it and go for the robot setup work instead.

say: I'd say this is **huge**, and anyone not planning is mad.
I'd post **what I'm doing** online so people have examples.
think: Two years is enough to start a business but not to **make it pay** before robots.
At **31** I'd have a truck licence and a hobby business.
do: Grow the **removals service** using AI for quotes, bookings and adverts.
Save the **installer money** without touching it.
Train to set up and fix **home robots** by 2030.
S2.quote: Two years is enough to set up something of my own, but not enough to make it pay before the robots turn up.
fieldNote: Kira sees the thinking-AI years as a **boost** for a tiny business.
She picks **savings** over the business when forced, showing a realist streak.
Her pivot target is **robot setup** work in homes.

steps.text: Grow the weekend removals service using AI for bookings
Save the installer pay and leave it untouched
Train to install and fix home robots by 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning, so use it. I'd encourage people to learn something new each year. I'd post my own progress online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is the sweet spot for me: long enough to build a little business, short enough that I can't get lazy about it. Robots around 2034 means I've got years of carrying left. I think I'd come out okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the installer course this year and grow the removals business slowly, maybe a second van by 2029. I'd keep investing 100 a month. By 2032 I'd look at whether to buy or rent robot helpers for the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good, busy way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A second van means borrowing. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only a small loan, and only if the bookings were steady for a year. My dad borrowed for a shop and lost it, so I'm careful. I'd rather grow slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marco?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to come in with me. He's strong and customers love him. He'd say no at first and then probably yes.

say: I'd say five years is a **decent warning**, so people should use it.
I'd encourage people to **learn something** new each year.
think: Five years is my **sweet spot** for building a business.
Robots around **2034** leave years of carrying work.
do: Grow the removals business to a **second van** by 2029.
Keep investing **100 a month** and weigh robot helpers by 2032.
feel: **Uneasy**, but in a good, busy way.
S3.quote: Five years is the sweet spot for me: long enough to build a little business, short enough that I can't get lazy about it.
fieldNote: Kira's **business plan** grows more ambitious with more time.
Her father's **failed shop** keeps her careful with loans.
She wants to bring her crewmate **Marco** into the business.

steps.text: Grow the removals business to a second van by 2029
Keep putting 100 a month into the index fund
Weigh buying robot helpers for the removals firm by 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads, so there's no excuse. I'd tell people to start small, like I did. I'd probably post a guide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Give me ten years and I'd be renting out the robots that carry sofas, not competing with them. Robots around 2039 means I'd be 40 with a business that's had a decade to grow. I think that's a good place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the delivery job for a few years, build the removals business on the side, and go full time when it pays a wage. I'd keep investing. Around 2037 I'd start trialling robot helpers on the jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could knock that calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A big company doing the same thing with robots cheaper than me. That could happen. Then I'd sell up and do something else, I'd have savings by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your own life to look like by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small business, a flat I own, maybe a partner. Not rich. Just not waiting for someone else to decide my job.

say: I'd say ten years is **loads**, so there's no excuse.
I'd tell people to **start small** and maybe post a guide.
think: With ten years I'd be **renting out robots**, not competing with them.
At **40** I'd have a business with a decade behind it.
do: Build the **removals business** on the side, going full time when it pays.
S4.quote: Give me ten years and I'd be renting out the robots that carry sofas, not competing with them.
fieldNote: Kira is one of the few who feels **calm** in an AGI picture.
Her risk is a **big company** undercutting her with robots.
She wants **control** over her own work more than wealth.

steps.text: Build the removals business until it pays a full wage
Trial robot helpers on removal jobs around 2037
Keep investing in the index fund each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's too fast for a small business to pay off before robots arrive. What would help is cheap small-business loans and short courses on setting up robots, so people like me can be part of it. Customers tip the person who carries the washing machine, not the app that booked the slot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who people think will own the robots. That's the question for me. If it's only big companies, people like me lose; if it's small firms too, we've got a chance.

headlineQuote: Customers tip the person who carries the washing machine, not the app that booked the slot.
portrait: Kira Farah, 27, drives a **furniture delivery** truck and sells ex-display furniture on the side.
She uses AI every day and sees Steady Disruption as an **opportunity**.
In the fast picture she's anxious, building **removals work** while carrying jobs remain.
With more time she plans to **own robot helpers** and feels calm about it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as it's too fast for a small business to pay off.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **small-business loans** and short courses on setting up robots.
